extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers (listeners of Writing Excuses)
extracted.subtask_description: Use the MICE quotient (Milieu, Inquiry, Character, Event) as an organizational tool to design, focus, and manage the conflicts in a story or scene. The page explains how each MICE element determines where a story starts and stops and what kinds of conflicts belong in the middle.

rubrics_metrics.name: MICE quotient (milieu, inquiry, character, event)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MICE quotient is an organizational theory that says that every story contains four elements—milieu, inquiry, character, and event—and which one of those is the major driver affects where your story starts and stops and the kinds of conflicts that go in the middle. You can have more than one, and then you can treat it kind of like nesting boxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MICE as a framing tool: identify which element is the dominant driver to determine story boundaries and the kinds of conflicts to include. Treat multiple elements as nested or interleaved threads; explicitly decide which is primary to avoid unfocused stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milieu stories: start on entering, end on exiting; conflicts prevent exit
rubrics_metrics.description: Milieu begins when a character enters a place and it ends when they exit. Every conflict your character is running into has to be something that prevents them from exiting the place, because the moment they do, the story is over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build sequences of impediments that block exit using try-fail cycles (yes/no, no-and escalation). Example: Star Wars 'retrieving the princess' sequence—each obstacle prevents escape until the exit happens and that part of the story closes. Note: milieu elements can coexist with other elements (character interpersonal stuff can interfere with escape).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry stories: driven by a question; end when the question is answered
rubrics_metrics.description: An inquiry story is driven by questions, starting with a question and ending when it is answered (murder mysteries are classic examples). The middle of the story consists of things that keep the protagonist from answering that question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design conflicts that block or misdirect the answer (false leads, missing evidence, overturned assumptions). Beware that answering one question can open bigger questions—keep threads related to the main inquiry or risk story bloat. Example: police-procedural 'act two body' as a try-fail complication. Avoid unrelated side conflicts unless intentionally layering multiple threads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character stories: about transformation; conflicts are interior
rubrics_metrics.description: Character stories are about character transformation or change (often begins unhappy and ends when the character has changed). The conflicts are things that get in the way of that change and are largely interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate the middle with internal barriers (doubt, self-loathing, failed attempts to change) and interpersonal forces resisting the change (friends who prefer the old self). Distinguish whether the character is driving the change or resisting it—this affects the shape of try-fail cycles. Common genres: coming-of-age, romance. When pairing with other MICE elements, consider how the character's inner arc may require sacrifice or conflict with external goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event stories: status quo broken; external conflicts and cascading consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Event stories start when the normal status quo gets broken in some way; the character tries to put it right. They revolve around external conflict and often introduce many changes that need resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume a single event equals a complete story—map the cascading changes and continue to reveal conflicts and discoveries throughout the story. Example: a ship hijacking (Zero G) is an event that creates ongoing conflicts; you must show how the event alters the world and creates multiple threads to resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining and nesting MICE threads (A/B plot considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can combine multiple MICE elements (A plot and B plot), which can make a story more interesting, but can also cause story bloat if threads are unrelated or if the only real conflict lives in the B plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave A and B plots so conflicts feel organic and related to the dominant driver. Watch out for the anti-pattern where an unrelated plot thread interrupts the main question/goal, creating unfocused middle material. Deliberately layered threads can be powerful if they interact; otherwise prune or integrate threads to avoid bloat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try–fail cycles and act-structure application
rubrics_metrics.description: Use try–fail cycles (attempt, fail, escalate) to populate the middle of the story—this is especially emphasized for milieu and character conflicts but applies broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure obstacles as successive yes/no or no-and escalations (try one thing—no; try another—no and it gets worse). Use classic act-two complications (e.g., 'act two body' in procedurals) as turns that reshape attempts. Ensure each failure raises stakes or insights leading toward eventual resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine story boundaries by dominant MICE element
rubrics_metrics.description: Which MICE element is the major driver affects where your story starts and stops (e.g., milieu starts on entering and ends on exiting; inquiry starts on the question and ends when answered; character ends when change occurs; event starts at the status-quo break).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the dominant element early to focus which conflicts belong in the middle and where the story should open and close. Use this to avoid misplaced scenes that don't obstruct the core goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical exercise / production guidance (homework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Free write a character doing something, then identify the MICE elements present; pick the dominant one (or two) and build additional conflicts that follow that element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask of your draft: is my character trying to navigate/escape a place (milieu)? Trying to answer a question (inquiry)? Trying to change themselves (character)? Trying to change the outside world/status quo (event)? Use that diagnosis to choose and expand conflicts that directly obstruct the core driver.
